video_title: The Vertical Income Statement, Row by Row
learning_objectives: Build an Income Statement from revenue through retained profit
Calculate gross profit and profit with a worked numeric example
Evaluate what profit shows and what it hides

visual_beats.directive: Van and installed fences fade in
Blank statement sheet unrolls
First revenue figure drops into place
Empty rows light up in sequence

scenes.voiceover_script: Picketline Fencing Co installs garden fences, but its owner cannot explain where the money went. Sales were busy all year, yet the bank balance barely moved. An Income Statement records income and all costs incurred to earn that income over a period, usually a year. It is built vertically, line by line, from revenue down to retained profit. Watch each figure drop into place like a fence post.

visual_beats.directive: Revenue card locks at the top
Material icons stack into cost of sales
Subtraction line draws downward
Gross profit counter locks at seventy-five thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Start at the top with revenue. Revenue is the income from selling goods or services during a period. Picketline billed one hundred twenty thousand dollars for fencing jobs last year. Cost of sales is the cost of the posts, rails, concrete and gates actually used on those jobs: forty-five thousand dollars. Subtract cost of sales from revenue. One hundred twenty thousand minus forty-five thousand gives gross profit of seventy-five thousand dollars.

elements.label: Fitter wages van fuel insurance and rent

visual_beats.directive: Expense icons line up in a row
Overheads total counts to thirty-eight thousand
Subtraction line sweeps across
Profit counter locks at thirty-seven thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Gross profit is made when revenue is greater than cost of sales. It shows the margin earned before overheads. Now subtract expenses, the fixed costs and overheads of the period. Picketline spent thirty-eight thousand dollars on fitter wages, van fuel, insurance and yard rent. Seventy-five thousand minus thirty-eight thousand leaves profit of thirty-seven thousand dollars. Profit is total income less total costs, and it rewards the owner for risk-taking.

visual_beats.directive: Profit counter reaches the first gate
Tax removes seven thousand
Dividends remove ten thousand
Retained profit reserves twenty thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Profit is not the same as cash in the owner's pocket. First deduct tax of seven thousand dollars. Thirty-seven thousand minus seven thousand leaves thirty thousand dollars. Then pay dividends of ten thousand dollars to the shareholders. Thirty thousand minus ten thousand leaves retained profit of twenty thousand dollars. Retained profit is the earnings kept in the business for growth, perhaps a second van or a wider stock of fencing materials.

visual_beats.directive: Profit tile branches into four outcomes
Retained profit flows to a new van icon
Borrowing tile shrinks as profit grows
Year labels scroll for comparison

scenes.voiceover_script: Why does profit matter? It is a reward for risk-taking and a source of finance for expansion. It measures success and attracts investors and lenders. Because retained profit can fund a new van, therefore the firm borrows less, so future interest costs fall. Comparing this Income Statement with last year's reveals whether material costs or overheads are rising. A falling profit warns the owner before the problem becomes a crisis.

elements.label: Revenue bar one hundred twenty thousand

visual_beats.directive: Revenue bar stretches across the frame
Cost segments peel away from the bar
Profit bar settles at about one third
Two-step formula card flashes

scenes.voiceover_script: Do not confuse revenue with profit. Revenue is the total sales income: one hundred twenty thousand dollars. Profit is what remains after costs: thirty-seven thousand dollars. On screen, the revenue bar stretches across the frame while the profit bar is only a fraction as long. A firm can grow revenue and still see profit shrink if costs rise faster. Always show the calculation in two steps: revenue minus cost of sales, then minus expenses.

on_screen_labels: Misses cash timing and asset value

visual_beats.directive: Left panel lists what profit reveals
Clock icon shows late customer payment
Asset and goodwill tiles stay hidden
Three statements sit side by side

scenes.voiceover_script: Now evaluate what profit does and does not show. It shows whether trading earned more than it cost, and it helps compare years. It does not show cash timing, so a profitable firm can still miss a supplier payment. It does not show the value of assets, the quality of fences or customer goodwill. Historic figures look backward. Use the Income Statement beside a cash-flow forecast and a statement of financial position before deciding.

visual_beats.directive: Top revenue row locks in
Gross profit and profit rows follow
Tax and dividend gates close
Retained profit seals the statement

scenes.voiceover_script: Let us rebuild the whole vertical statement in one pass. Revenue one hundred twenty thousand; cost of sales forty-five thousand; gross profit seventy-five thousand; expenses thirty-eight thousand; profit thirty-seven thousand; tax seven thousand; dividends ten thousand; retained profit twenty thousand. Each row locks into place like a completed panel. The advantage is clarity; the limitation is that one period never tells the whole story of a fencing business. Compare several years before judging performance.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Picketline's revenue rose from $120,000 to $132,000 while cost of sales rose from $45,000 to $56,250. What happened to gross profit?
options: It rose from $75,000 to $75,750, but the gross margin fell
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: Both revenue bars grow; the red cost segment expands faster in percentage terms, the green gross-profit segment grows only from $75,000 to $75,750, and a margin dial turns down from 62.50% to 57.39%.
